title: Correcting a Reason: No es que… sino que…

sections.title: Reject one reason, give the real one
sections.content: You know *sino* and *sino que* from B1 Unit 40, and the subjunctive after doubt, as in *dudo que*, from B1 Unit 13. New here is a pattern for correcting a reason: *No es que* + subjunctive, *sino que* + indicative. It rejects a reason that someone might assume and gives the real one: *No es que no quiera, sino que no puedo* means 'It is not that I don't want to, it is that I can't.'

sections.title: Why the moods differ
sections.content: The first part names a reason you say is *not* the case. You are not stating it as a fact, so the verb is in the subjunctive, as after *no creo que*. The second part gives the true reason, which you do state as a fact, so after *sino que* the verb is in the indicative. *Sino que* always keeps its *que*, because a conjugated verb follows (B1 Unit 40).

sections.title: Same pattern, three tenses
rows: No es que no quiera, sino que no puedo.
It is not that I don't want to, it is that I can't.
No es que esté enojado, sino que estoy cansado.
It is not that I am angry, it is that I am tired.
No era que no me gustara, sino que no tenía tiempo.
It was not that I didn't like it, it was that I had no time. (past: imperfect subjunctive, then imperfect)

items.spanish: No es que no quiera ir, sino que no puedo.
items.english: It is not that I do not want to go, but that I cannot.

items.spanish: No es que Marta esté enojada, sino que está cansada.
items.english: It is not that Marta is angry, it is that she is tired.

items.spanish: No es que no me guste el trabajo, sino que gano poco.
items.english: It is not that I dislike the job, but that I earn little.

items.spanish: No era que Pablo no quisiera ayudar, sino que no sabía cómo.
items.english: It was not that Pablo did not want to help, but that he did not know how.

items.spanish: No es que tenga miedo, sino que prefiero esperar.
items.english: It is not that I am afraid, it is that I prefer to wait.

sections.content: Use this pattern when you expect someone to draw a wrong conclusion. It is a kind way to disagree, because you correct a reason, not a person. *Pero* would only add a limit to what you said; *sino que* replaces the wrong reason with the right one.
